blocks.text: Annihilation occurs whenever a particle and its antiparticle come close together: the pair disappears and its mass-energy appears as photons. Mass-energy and momentum are conserved in the process. The annihilation of an electron-positron pair was discussed in the previous chapter.

In elementary-particle research very high energies are needed, so instead of colliding particles at their rest-mass energies, they are accelerated to nearly the speed of light and then collided. At CERN's Large Hadron Collider (LHC), protons and other nuclei are collided at nearly the speed of light to recreate conditions like those of the early universe; collisions at energies of the order of TeV give insight into those conditions. In such collisions the W+, W- and Z bosons, the particles that carry the electroweak force, predicted by Professor Abdus Salam, have been discovered, along with the top and bottom quarks and, most significantly, the Higgs boson in July 2012.

blocks.title: The LHC collides protons with protons
blocks.text: The book describes proton-antiproton collisions at the LHC. The LHC collides protons with protons (and heavy nuclei such as lead with each other); proton-antiproton collisions were made at the earlier Tevatron and at CERN's older SPS, where the W and Z bosons were first found in 1983. The book's own photograph caption describes a 7 TeV proton-proton collision in the CMS detector.

Calculate the energy of the gamma-ray photons emitted in the annihilation of an electron-positron pair at rest. Solution: the masses of the positron and the electron are each 9.1 x 10^-31 kg. By Einstein's relation, E = 2mc^2 = 2 x 9.1 x 10^-31 kg x (3 x 10^8 m s^-1)^2 = 1.64 x 10^-13 J. In electron volts, E = 1.64 x 10^-13 / 1.6 x 10^-19 = 1.02 MeV. Two gamma-ray photons are emitted, each of 0.51 MeV, travelling in opposite directions to conserve momentum.

blocks.alt: Left: an electron and a positron move towards each other and annihilate, sending two gamma photons of 0.51 MeV in opposite directions; E = 2moc^2 = 1.02 MeV shared by two photons. Right: a PET scanner; a patient lies inside a ring of detectors, and a dashed line through an annihilation point inside the body shows two gamma rays travelling in opposite directions to detectors on opposite sides of the ring.
blocks.caption: Annihilation and PET scanning (original diagram).
blocks.long_description: Because the two photons leave in exactly opposite directions, detecting both at once tells the scanner the line on which the annihilation happened; many such lines build up an image of where the tracer is.

blocks.text: The gamma-ray photons from an annihilation inside the body have enough energy to travel out of the body, so they can be detected outside it. This is used in positron emission tomography (PET): a tracer that emits positrons is introduced into the body; each positron soon meets an electron and annihilates, and the two 0.51 MeV gamma rays travelling in opposite directions are detected by a ring of detectors around the patient.

blocks.prompt: Why are the two photons from electron-positron annihilation emitted in opposite directions?
blocks.explanation: The pair has (almost) zero total momentum before annihilation, so to conserve momentum the two photons must carry equal and opposite momenta: equal energies (0.51 MeV each) in opposite directions.

items: Annihilation: particle + antiparticle -> photons; mass-energy and momentum conserved.
e- + e+ -> two 0.51 MeV gamma rays in opposite directions (E = 2mc^2 = 1.02 MeV).
LHC research: W, Z (predicted by Abdus Salam), Higgs boson (2012); PET uses annihilation.
